newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Menem signs decree ordering airports privatization.
newsitem.headline: Menem signs decree ordering airports privatization.

text.p: President Carlos Menem Thursday signed a decree ordering the privatization of Argentina's main airports, local news agencies reported.

The private DyN new agency quoted Cabinet chief Jorge Rodriguez as saying the decree envisages the sell-off of 28 national and provincial terminals "immediately," with more sales of the country's 53 airports at a later stage.
The decree will allow the government to receive $250 million in the near future which Rodriguez said were necessary for the maintenance of the country's major airports.
The Menem administration expects the move will bring in total investments of $2.0 billion over the next three decades.

More than 20 international companies, including firms from the United States, Italy, Britain, France and Ireland have expressed interest in the privatization, in which Union Bank of Switzerland is acting as advisor to the government.
Government officials will embark on road shows to ensure major international investors get to know the details.

The government opted for concessions because the law does not allow a sell-off when it is done by presidential decree rather than congressional law. It was not immediately clear how long the concessions would last.

The government originally planned last year to sell most airports, but Menem's government was unable to push the bill through a reluctant lower chamber of Congress and eventually settled for a scaled-down version of fewer terminals and concessions instead of sales.

Rodriguez said earlier this week that plans to build an airport on an artificial island on the River Plate to replace both Ezeiza and Aeroparque terminals in Buenos Aires have not been scrapped but would now become a decision for the future concessionaires to take.
The president embarked on an ambitious privatization drive soon after first taking office in 1989, selling off everything from utilities to railroads, airlines, ports and highways.
The airports, along with the country's nuclear plants and hydroelectric dams, are some of the few remaining state-owned firms not yet handed over to private hands.
